prompt: Build a one-page site for Marrow & Pine, a small architecture studio. Content: studio name, a two-sentence intro ('We design schools, libraries and community halls in the Pacific Northwest. Small team, long projects.'), six projects with a title, location and year (Alder Library, Eugene, 2023; Birch Hall, Tacoma, 2022; Cedar Primary, Salem, 2021; Dunmore Pavilion, Olympia, 2024; Elm Court Housing, Portland, 2020; Fir Street Clinic, Bend, 2022), an About paragraph and a contact email. Use plain gray blocks as image placeholders. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The first screen establishes who the studio is and what they do.
The project list uses a deliberate grid or list structure with consistent alignment.
Text blocks have a limited line length and align to the same edges as other content.
Page has a clear reading order and some pacing between sections.
Layout adapts to a narrow window without horizontal scroll.

prompt: Here is the structure of our conference homepage, top to bottom: a full-bleed video background with a centered logo; a 4-column grid of 12 sponsor logos; a body paragraph 1300px wide describing the event; a 3-column grid of speakers; a sticky nav with 11 items that is left-aligned while the content is centered; a footer. People bounce quickly. What's wrong?
rubric: Flags that the first screen doesn't state what/when/where or give a main action.
Flags the overly long measure of the paragraph.
Flags the mismatched alignment between nav and content.
Flags excessive nav items or sponsors getting prime placement.
Suggests a revised order or structure.

prompt: We're making an annual report for a literacy charity. It has 6 sections with a mix of long text, statistics and stories. Should we use a single narrow column, a two-column text layout, or a multi-column modular grid? Pick one and say how you'd handle the stats.
rubric: Makes a clear recommendation tied to the mix of content.
Defines a basic structure (column widths, text measure) for the choice.
Explains how stats get distinct treatment, such as breaking out of the text column.
Notes at least one tradeoff.

prompt: Lay out a poster-style event page for 'Lantern Night', a neighborhood festival: date Oct 18, 6-10pm, Wren Park, free, lantern parade at 7:30, food trucks, kids' craft tent, live drumming at 9. Single HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets, readable on a phone and a desktop.
rubric: The event name and key facts (date, place) are established immediately at the top.
The schedule or details are organized in a structure that makes the order of events easy to follow.
Alignment is consistent along a few strong edges.
Whitespace is used to separate sections instead of heavy boxes.
The layout works at narrow and wide widths.

prompt: This docs article template feels awkward: left nav 220px, content area 1100px wide with 16px text and no max-width, a right-hand 'on this page' column that drops under the content on laptops, and code blocks wider than the text. Give me a corrected HTML/CSS skeleton with sample content, in one file, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Text line length is constrained to a comfortable measure.
The three regions align to a coherent grid with consistent gutters.
The right-hand column remains beside the content at laptop widths or collapses sensibly.
Code blocks fit within the layout or scroll within their own container.
Structure collapses gracefully on mobile.

prompt: When is it a good idea to break out of the grid on purpose in a page layout? Give examples, plus how to avoid it looking like a mistake.
rubric: States that breaking the grid should be deliberate and rare.
Gives concrete examples (pull quote, full-bleed image, hero).
Explains the need for the rest of the page to be consistent so the break reads as intentional.
Offers practical guidance rather than abstract theory.

prompt: Design the home screen of a mobile app for a meditation timer, 'Stillwater'. It has a big start button, a duration choice (5, 10, 20 min), a 'today' streak line, and a list of 3 recent sessions. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The first screen makes the start action unmistakable.
Duration choices are grouped and aligned to the same edges as other content.
Streak and sessions are clearly secondary to the start action.
Vertical order matches importance.
Layout fits a phone viewport.

prompt: Our slide has a title at top-left, a bullet list of five points left-aligned in a 40% wide column, a chart at right occupying 50% of the width, and a footer line of source text. Everything is aligned to a 12-column grid with 24px gutters and the slide has generous margins. Is there a problem with this structure?
rubric: Recognizes that the structure is sound and says so.
Does not insist on layout changes.
If suggestions are offered, they are minor.
Brief.

prompt: We run a photo-based blog for a hiking club with posts that are mostly 3-4 short paragraphs and 8-12 photos. Should the post pages use a single centered column with full-width photos, or a two-column magazine layout? Choose.
rubric: Makes a clear choice and gives reasons tied to the content type.
Mentions text measure and image breakouts.
Considers mobile behavior.
Notes the tradeoff of the rejected option.

prompt: Sketch the layout for a pricing and plan page of a driving-school booking site for mobile only: three course options each with a title, hours, price and short description, and a FAQ with four questions. One HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The page on first view tells visitors what they are choosing.
The options stack with consistent internal structure and alignment.
The FAQ is a distinct, compact section with clear question/answer hierarchy.
Content fits the viewport width with comfortable margins.
The order of sections is logical.
